newsitem.title: CHINA: Grand Old Lady peaks early for her birthday.
newsitem.headline: Grand Old Lady peaks early for her birthday.

text.p: The Grand Old Lady of Hong Kong decided on Wednesday to celebrate her 70th birthday early and join in the China handover celebrations.
Clark Gable, Richard Nixon and Elton John have enjoyed her hospitality. She even has her own helipad and boasts a fleet of luxury Rolls-Royce cars.
The Peninsula hotel, a Hong Kong icon since 1928, decided to launch its birthday celebrations early with the release of a glossy history of its chequered past.

"We wanted to be part of the handover celebrations. So many of our regular guests have been coming back. This is the ideal time," a hotel spokeswoman explained at the launch of "Portrait of a Grand Old Lady" by Canadian author Frances Bartlett.
She recounts how the hotel, known fondly to its fans as "The Pen", acted as headquarters for the Japanese occupying forces after they swept into Hong Kong in World War Two.
Clark Gable taught the barman how to make screwdriver cocktails. Waiter Wong Wai once politely but firmly told flamboyant rock star Elton John to obey hotel etiquette and remove his hat in the lobby.
Former president Richard Nixon, forced from office by the Watergate scandal and his infamous White House tapes, spotted a young tourist fiddling with his new tape recorder in the lobby.
He walked over and growled: "Be careful with that, son. One of those got me into big trouble."

The Fanling Hunt Club held its annual ball at the hotel. Staff were once caught running a casino in their roof quarters. A guest asked for rose petals to be scattered on his bed in the shape of a heart.

As Hong Kong wound up a five-day holiday marking the handover of the British colony to China, people eagerly queued to enjoy the ritual of afternoon tea with sultana-studded scones covered in lashings of Devonshire cream.
Up in the gallery overlooking the Renaissance-style lobby, a classical string quartet played selections from Strauss.
After almost 70 years, it still looks like a stage set for a Somerset Maugham novel. You could imagine debonair entertainer Noel Coward tinkling away at the piano.
The book certainly falls prey to some purple prose in recreating the Peninsula's past but it does neatly encapsulate the essence of subtle service.
A gentleman guest returned to the hotel weighed down with shopping plunder. An attendant carefully hung up the new shirts and suits and then spotted a new pair of shoes.
Holding them carefully in the palm of his hand, the room attendant inquired: "And would Sir like his shoes walked?"
